470.title: Count the cost (Luke 14:25–33)
470.hook: a builder sits down to reckon before building a tower
470.howItsDone: Catholics preparing for baptism, marriage, ordination or religious vows go through a period of formation and discernment, so that, as Luke puts it, they sit down and count the cost before they promise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a great supper, three thin excuses, and a house filled from the roadsides. Your line was compel them to come in.

On the edge of town sits a half-built house. The foundation poured, the frame up, and then nothing. Weeds in the yard, plywood going gray, a for-sale sign that's been there three summers. The house tells its own story: somebody started and ran out of money. Jesus has great crowds walking with him on the road now. You'd think he'd be glad. Instead he turns around and says something that sounds almost designed to thin the crowd.
screen: `THE HALF-BUILT HOUSE IN TOWN.` → `SOMEBODY RAN OUT OF MONEY.` → `HE TURNS TO THE CROWD.`

segments.voice: First the hard sentence. If anyone comes to me and hates not his father and mother, and wife and children, and brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. It's meant to stop you. Matthew's Gospel helps here: it gives the saying as, he that loves father or mother more than me. So readers hear hate as a way of speaking by contrast: loving one thing so much less than another that it looks like hate beside it. Jesus isn't canceling the commandment to honor your parents. He's asking what comes first. Then two pictures. "For which of you having a mind to build a tower, doth not first sit down, and reckon the charges that are necessary, whether he have wherewithal to finish it." Otherwise he lays the foundation, can't finish, and everyone laughs: this man began to build and was not able to finish. Second picture: a king with ten thousand soldiers hears another king is coming with twenty thousand. Doesn't he sit down first and think? If he can't win, he sends an embassy and asks for peace. Then the conclusion: every one of you that does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple. Jesus isn't hiding the price to close the sale. He tells the crowd: sit down first, and count it. And notice the word sit. Both the builder and the king sit down. In both pictures, deciding is done slowly, sitting down, with the numbers in front of you.

segments.voice: Pick one thing you've said yes to, or are about to, a job, a relationship, a ministry, a promise, and sit with it the way the builder sits with his plans. Name honestly what it will take, time, money, sleep, pride, and ask whether you have enough to finish, and what would help. If you pray, ask for wisdom and for what you lack.
Renounce. Jesus' warning to the crowds: sit down like a builder or a king and reckon what following him will take before you begin. Today's word.
Your line: sit down and reckon. No hidden price, no fine print. See you tomorrow.

471.title: The clever steward (Luke 16:1–13)
471.hook: a crooked manager is praised for being shrewd; you can't serve God and mammon
471.howItsDone: Catholics often speak of stewardship, the idea that time, talent and money are entrusted by God rather than owned outright, and some parishes ask members to make an annual stewardship commitment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a builder sat down to count before he built his tower. Your line was sit down and reckon.

A manager is caught wasting his boss's money. He's about to be fired. So he spends his last afternoon cooking the books in his customers' favor. And at the end of the story, the boss praises him. This is a parable preachers sometimes approach carefully, and readers still argue about parts of it. It sounds like Jesus is applauding fraud. He isn't. To see what he is doing, watch the manager's hands.
screen: `A PARABLE READERS STILL ARGUE ABOUT.` → `CAUGHT WASTING THE BOSS'S MONEY.` → `AND THE BOSS PRAISES HIM.`

segments.voice: A rich man hears his steward has wasted his goods. He calls him in: give an account, you're done. The steward thinks fast. I can't dig, I'm ashamed to beg. I know what I'll do, so that people will take me into their homes. He calls in his master's debtors one by one. How much do you owe? A hundred barrels of oil. Sit down quickly, write fifty. And you? A hundred quarters of wheat. Write eighty. He's making friends with the only currency he has left. Then the surprise: "And the lord commended the unjust steward, forasmuch as he had done wisely: for the children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light." Notice what's praised. Not the dishonesty; he's still called unjust. He saw the end coming and acted. He knew his position wouldn't last, and he used what was passing through his hands to make friends who would. Jesus draws the lesson: make friends with the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, when your own time runs out, they may receive you into everlasting dwellings. Mammon is the Douay's word for wealth, money and property. In the Catholic reading, everyone is a steward like this one, who will one day be asked to give an account. So use it now, while it's in your hands, for people. Then the line the passage ends on: "You cannot serve God and mammon." No servant can serve two masters.

segments.voice: Picture what's passing through your hands this week, a paycheck, an allowance, a budget, even a few dollars, and notice that none of it stays. Think of one person you could do some good for with a small part of it: a coworker's lunch, a friend's coffee, a family that's struggling. If you pray, ask to be a faithful steward.

472.title: Lazarus at the gate (Luke 16:19–31)
472.hook: a rich man never noticed the beggar at his own gate
472.howItsDone: Catholics hear the parable of the rich man and Lazarus at Sunday Mass in the year of Luke's Gospel, and popes, Paul VI and Francis among them, have used it to speak about the rich and the poor in today's world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a crooked steward used his last afternoon to make friends with his master's money. Your line was god or mammon.

Things right at your door can become invisible exactly because they're always there: the recycling bin, the neighbor's car, maybe a person sitting against the wall of the corner store you pass every day. Jesus tells a parable about two men separated by a single gate. One lives behind it in luxury. The other lies just outside it, every day. One of them has a name in the story. It's not the rich one.
screen: `WHAT'S OUTSIDE YOUR FRONT DOOR?` → `ALWAYS THERE, SO INVISIBLE.` → `TWO MEN, ONE GATE.`

segments.voice: Luke paints the rich man in two strokes: clothed in purple and fine linen, feasting sumptuously every day. Purple dye was ruinously expensive, the color of kings. Then the other man: "And there was a certain beggar, named Lazarus, who lay at his gate, full of sores." He longs for the crumbs from the table, and the dogs come and lick his sores. Of all the people Jesus invents for his parables, Lazarus is the only one given a name. Abraham and Moses appear here too, but they come from Scripture. Later Latin readers called the rich man Dives, but that's just the Latin word for rich. Both men die. Lazarus is carried by angels to Abraham's bosom. The rich man is in torment, and now he looks up and sees Lazarus. He knows his name. He knew it all along. He asks Abraham to send Lazarus with a drop of water, as if Lazarus were still a servant. Abraham answers gently, calling him son, and says a great chaos is now fixed between them. One more request: send Lazarus to warn my five brothers. Abraham says: they have Moses and the prophets. Let them hear them. If they won't, they won't believe even if someone rises from the dead. The rich man is never accused of hurting Lazarus, never cruel to him. His sin is simpler and more common: Lazarus was at his gate every day, and he stepped around him. The chasm after death is just the gate made permanent.

segments.voice: Walk in your mind along the route you take every day, front door, street, store, office, the screen you scroll, and ask who is there every day that you've stopped seeing. Let one person come into focus: someone sitting outside, a lonely neighbor, a coworker who eats alone. If you pray, pray for them, by name if you know it.
Lazarus. The poor man with a name, lying every day at the door of a rich man who stepped around him. Today's word.
Your line: he was at the gate. Every day, a name, right there. Day four hundred seventy-two, in the books.

473.title: One came back (Luke 17:11–19)
473.hook: ten lepers healed, and one, a Samaritan, returns to say thank you
473.howItsDone: Catholics call the Mass the Eucharist, from the Greek for thanksgiving, and some make a short prayer of thanksgiving in silence after receiving Communion before leaving the church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a rich man stepped around Lazarus every day. Your line was he was at the gate.

A birthday is over, and a parent stands over a child with a pen and a stack of cards: write your thank-you notes. To the child, it's a chore. A thank-you that arrives days later, unasked, saying what you did for me mattered, is a different thing. Jesus is still on the road to Jerusalem, passing between Samaria and Galilee. At the edge of a village, ten men stand far off, because their disease means they have to keep their distance.
screen: `WRITE YOUR THANK-YOU NOTES.` → `SOMEONE CAME BACK TO SAY IT.` → `TEN MEN STANDING FAR OFF.`

segments.voice: They lift up their voices: Jesus, master, have mercy on us. In the Law of Moses, leprosy names a range of skin conditions, and Leviticus says the person must dwell alone, outside the camp, and cry out that he is unclean. Jesus doesn't touch them this time. He just says: go, show yourselves to the priests. That's what the Law required when someone was healed, so the priest could declare them clean and they could go home. And as they went, they were cleansed. Nine keep walking, doing exactly what Jesus told them. "And one of them, when he saw that he was made clean, went back, with a loud voice glorifying God." He falls on his face at Jesus' feet, giving thanks. And Luke adds: and this was a Samaritan. The outsider. Jesus asks, almost to himself: "Were not ten made clean? and where are the nine?" He calls the man a stranger, the only one who came back to give glory to God. Then: arise, go thy way, thy faith hath made thee whole. Here's what a Catholic ear catches. Luke's Greek word for giving thanks is eucharistein, the word behind Eucharist, the name Catholics give the Mass itself. Some Catholic readers see the Samaritan, face down on the road, as a small picture of that: a healed man who turns around and gives thanks. The nine weren't bad. They were obedient. They were also in a hurry to get back to their lives.

Choose one, and get specific about what exactly they did and what difference it made; if you pray, give thanks to God for them too.

474.title: The persistent widow (Luke 18:1–8)
474.hook: she wears down an unjust judge; pray always and don't lose heart
474.howItsDone: Catholics often pray for one intention over many days, as in a novena, nine days of prayer; Saint Monica, whose feast is August 27, is honored as a patron of those who pray for a long time for a loved one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ten were healed, and the Samaritan came back. Your line was where are the nine.

A town, a courtroom, and a judge who, Jesus says, "feared not God, nor regarded man." Nothing moves him: not heaven, not what people say. Into his court comes a widow with a case against someone who has wronged her. The story mentions no money, no family, no one to speak for her. She has one weapon: she keeps showing up. And before the story even starts, Luke tells us what it's for.
screen: `A JUDGE WHO FEARS NO ONE.` → `A WIDOW WITH A CASE.` → `ONE WEAPON: SHE KEEPS SHOWING UP.`

segments.voice: Here's that opening line in the Douay-Rheims: "And he spoke also a parable to them, that we ought always to pray, and not to faint." Faint here means lose heart, give up. The widow keeps coming: avenge me of my adversary. For a while he won't. Then he talks to himself, and it's almost funny. Although I don't fear God or respect anyone, yet because this widow is a bother to me, I'll give her justice, "lest continually coming she weary me." The Greek verb behind weary me is a fighter's word: literally, to strike under the eye. Some readers hear the judge half joking: if I don't rule for her, she'll come in here and give me a black eye. Either way, a widow with nothing wins by refusing to stop. Then Jesus draws the line. If an unjust judge gives in to persistence, how much more will God, who isn't unjust at all, do justice for his chosen who cry to him day and night? It's an argument from the lesser to the greater: God is the opposite of this judge. And a question hangs in the air: when the Son of man comes, will he find faith on earth? Catholic tradition offers a saint who lived this parable: Monica. For years she prayed for her son Augustine, who was living far from the faith. A bishop told her, as Augustine writes in his Confessions, that the son of so many tears could not be lost. Augustine became a bishop and a doctor of the Church.

Bring it once more, plainly, without dressing it up, the way the widow walked into court one more time. If you pray, ask again; if you don't, hold the hope steady for a moment without letting it go.

475.title: The publican (Luke 18:9–14)
475.hook: O God, be merciful to me a sinner, and he went home justified
475.howItsDone: At the Confiteor near the start of Mass, Catholics strike their breast, and some pray the Jesus Prayer, built in part on the publican's words, slowly with the breath; Eastern Christians may pray it on a prayer rope.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a widow wore down an unjust judge by never stopping. Your line was don't lose heart.

Luke tells us who this story is for before he tells it: some people who trusted in themselves as just, and despised others. That's not a description of one group. It's a habit, and it can belong to anybody: the scrolling that ends with at least I'm not like them. Two men go up to the Temple to pray at the same time. One is a Pharisee, careful and devout. The other is a publican, a tax collector, the kind of man the first one looks down on.
screen: `WHO THE STORY IS FOR.` → `AT LEAST I'M NOT LIKE THEM.` → `TWO MEN GO UP TO PRAY.`

segments.voice: First the Pharisee. The parable isn't a verdict on Pharisees as a whole, and this one is genuinely devout. He says: "O God, I give thee thanks that I am not as the rest of men", and then the list: not extortioners, unjust, adulterers, nor even like this publican. I fast twice in the week. I give tithes of all that I possess. Those are real practices, and real discipline. The trouble isn't what he does. It's the comparison: he's praying with one eye on God and one eye on the man in the back. Now the publican. He stands far off and won't even lift his eyes to heaven. He strikes his breast and says: "O God, be merciful to me a sinner." No list, no comparison, no excuses. Just the truth and a request. And Jesus says: "this man went down into his house justified rather than the other." Justified means set right with God. Then the line we heard at the dinner table: everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he that humbles himself shall be exalted. The publican's prayer has had a long life. At Mass, during the Confiteor, people strike their breast, an echo of his gesture. And the Catechism links his cry, and the blind man's, to the Jesus Prayer, prayed in the East and the West: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner.
screen: `I AM NOT AS THE REST OF MEN.` · `FASTING, TITHING, AND COMPARING.` · `HE STRIKES HIS BREAST.` · `HE WENT HOME JUSTIFIED.` · then, large: `O GOD, BE MERCIFUL TO ME A SINNER.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes lower, the way his did, and notice if your mind starts making a list, of your good deeds or of other people's faults; let the list go. If you pray, say his words slowly with your breath, O God as you breathe in, be merciful to me a sinner as you breathe out; if you don't, simply sit with honesty about yourself, without comparing.
The publican. The tax collector at the back of the Temple who prayed eight words without comparing, and went home justified. Today's word.
Your line: be merciful to me. Eight words of his, still in use. See you tomorrow.

476.title: The pounds (Luke 19:11–27)
476.hook: servants given money to trade while the master is away
476.howItsDone: Catholics speak of the gifts given to every baptized person and of using them in service, and some parishes ask members to share their gifts, from music to accounting to visiting the sick.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a publican at the back of the Temple asked for mercy and went home justified. Your line was be merciful to me.

Jesus is nearly at Jerusalem now. He's just been to Jericho, where a short tax collector named Zacheus climbed a sycamore to see him. The crowd is buzzing. Luke says they thought the kingdom of God was about to appear immediately, any minute now. So Jesus tells them a story about waiting. A nobleman goes to a far country to receive a kingdom and come back. Before he leaves, he calls ten servants and hands each one the same small sum of money.
screen: `NEARLY AT JERUSALEM.` → `THE KINGDOM, ANY MINUTE NOW.` → `A STORY ABOUT WAITING.`

segments.voice: Each servant gets one pound. The Greek word is mina: a real sum of money, though the master will later call it a little. The instruction in the Douay is short: "Trade till I come." Then his citizens send a message after him: we will not have this man to reign over us. Some readers hear an echo there: Josephus tells of a son of Herod who went to Rome to have his rule confirmed, with a delegation following to oppose him. The master comes back a king anyway and calls in his servants. The first: your pound has gained ten pounds. "Well done, good servant, because thou hast been faithful in a little, thou shalt have power over ten cities." The second has made five, and gets five cities. Then a third comes with his pound wrapped in a napkin. I was afraid of you, he says; you're an austere man, you take up what you didn't lay down. So I kept it safe. The master's answer is sharp: then why didn't you at least put it in the bank? The pound is taken from him and given to the one who has ten. The third servant didn't steal. He didn't waste. He just never used it, because he was afraid. Everyone started with the same pound; the difference was what they did with it while the master was away. Some Catholic readers take the pound as what everyone receives alike: faith, the word, the life of grace. Matthew tells a similar parable with talents, different amounts to each. Luke's version says: you all got the same gift.
screen: `ONE POUND EACH, THE SAME FOR ALL.` · `WE WILL NOT HAVE THIS MAN.` · `FAITHFUL IN A LITTLE.` · `WRAPPED IN A NAPKIN, OUT OF FEAR.` · then, large: `TRADE TILL I COME.`

segments.voice: Think of something you're good at, or were given, that you've kept wrapped in a napkin: a voice you don't sing with anymore, a language you stopped speaking, patience, humor, a knack for fixing things. Notice the fear that keeps it wrapped, and picture unwrapping it once, for someone else. If you pray, thank God for the gift.
The pounds. Ten servants, one coin each, told to trade until the master returns; the one who buried his out of fear loses it. Today's word.
Your line: trade with it. That's week sixty-eight: renounce, mammon, Lazarus, Samaritan, unjust judge, the publican, and the pounds. Day four hundred seventy-six, in the books.
